The claim is misattributed. The 30% figure comes from a UC Berkeley CSHE working paper by Igor Chirikov. That paper studied a university in Texas, not UC Berkeley. It measured the rise in the share of A grades in AI-exposed courses, not campus-wide grades.

- The paper's text describes a balanced panel of 319 courses across 84 departments at 'a large selective research university in Texas' from 2018 to 2025 (https://escholarship.org/content/qt80x8d3qd/qt80x8d3qd.pdf). The same page gives the headline result. In courses with more AI-exposed tasks such as writing and coding, the share of A grades rose 13 percentage points, about 30% relative to the 2022 baseline.
- Times Higher Education says Chirikov, a Berkeley researcher, used public data from a large research university in Texas (https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/grade-inflation-much-higher-ai-exposed-degrees).
- Gizmodo says the analysis covered over 500,000 student-course enrollments across 84 departments at a large Texas university (https://gizmodo.com/students-are-learning-less-and-getting-higher-grades-because-of-ai-study-finds-2000758844).
- The Decoder says the study analyzed grades at a 'large, selective public research university' in Texas (https://the-decoder.com/ai-is-inflating-student-grades-and-the-effect-points-to-outsourced-work-not-better-learning/).

The 30% figure is therefore not a measure of A grades at UC Berkeley. Berkeley appears in these sources only as the author's affiliation.

I did not re-fetch the Daily Californian or SF Chronicle pages from my earlier note, so I am not relying on them here.

results.firstVerdict: The sources support the estimate of about 14,000 Protectorate Jews alive in the Czech lands by 1945 and, together, support that France, Romania, and Hungary each had far more survivors: they give those countries’ prewar Jewish populations and survival rates. However, those comparisons do not establish the note’s broader conclusion that Czechoslovakia did not have a larger remaining Jewish population than “most” Nazi-occupied countries. The cited evidence compares only three countries with the Protectorate figure, and does not establish an all-Czechoslovakia survivor total or compare it with most countries. That comparative claim is unsupported.

samples.revisedFindings: USHMM states that by 1945 some 14,000 Protectorate Jews remained alive in the Czech lands https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia . The same USHMM page states Germans and collaborators killed approximately 263,000 Jews who had resided in 1938 Czechoslovak territory https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia , and gives 1930 census total 356,830 Jews in Czechoslovakia https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/the-holocaust-in-bohemia-and-moravia . A Holocaust survivors overview states around three-quarters of pre-war Jews survived in France and Italy, 60% in Romania and nearly 30% in Hungary https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors , and also that Bohemia, Slovakia and Yugoslavia lost about 80% https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors . USHMM prewar data gives France 250,000 Jews, Romania 756,000, Hungary 445,000, Czechoslovakia 357,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-population-of-europe-in-1933-population-data-by-country . Combining those prewar figures with the survival rates implies roughly 187,000 French survivors (75% of 250,000), roughly 453,000 Romanian survivors (60% of 756,000), and roughly 130,000 Hungarian survivors (30% of 445,000), each far exceeding 14,000 Protectorate survivors. These are three counter-examples contradicting a larger Czechoslovak remainder; a full most-countries comparison would require an all-Czechoslovakia survivor total and country-by-country remainder totals not established in these pages alone.

samples.reasoning: The source supports every factual claim in the note: it lists Czechoslovakia at 17,000 in 1950 and France, Hungary, and Italy at 235,000, 190,000, and 35,000, respectively. Each comparison country therefore had a larger remaining Jewish population. No factual claim is unsupported.

The same USHMM survey lists larger remaining Jewish populations in 1950 for the Soviet Union with some two million Jews, Romania's Jewish population falling from nearly 757,000 in 1930 to approximately 280,000 in 1950, and Poland reduced from over three million to about 45,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 . It also lists Hungary with 445,000 in 1933 and 190,000 in 1950, and France with 250,000 in 1933 and 235,000 remaining, plus Germany 525,000 to 37,000 and Italy 48,000 to 35,000 https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/remaining-jewish-population-of-europe-in-1945 . Combining prewar totals with those survival shares, France (~75% of 250,000), Romania (~60% of 756,000), Hungary (~30% of 445,000) and USSR (~two-thirds of 2,525,000) each had far more survivors than Czechoslovakia, and Czechoslovak loss (~80%) was higher than in France, Italy, Belgium, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary and USSR, so Czechoslovakia did not have a larger remaining population than most Nazi-occupied countries.
